newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish C/A gap seen $300 mln in 96, $3.9 bln in 97.
newsitem.headline: Polish C/A gap seen $300 mln in 96, $3.9 bln in 97.

text.p: Poland's current account is likely to close with a gap of some $300 million in 1996 after an almost $5 billion surplus in 1995, and widen to a $3.89 billion deficit in 1997, the government said in its 1997 budget draft.
It said exports will likely have grown about 9.5 percent by the end of this year against 35 percent last year while imports will likely have grown 28 percent against 38.9 percent in 1995.

The government estimates that revenue from exports next year will be 15 percent higher than this year thanks to the improving business climate among Poland's biggest trade partners, notably Germany. @

It also notes that exports will be propelled by foreign direct investment from previous years and higher productivity. But it said Polish exports could be threatened by high domestic inflation and wage growth exceeding productivity growth.
The draft assumes imports in 1997 would rise 21 percent against 1996 and it is expected to be dominated by investment goods and supplies on the back of Poland's economic growth.
"The lower import duties and scrapping of the import tax will relatively make imports less expensive, cutting production costs and, therefore, inflation," the draft said. @
On the strength of the higher imports the registered trade gap in 1997 is expected to baloon to $9.46 billion against this year's estimated $6.58 billion and last year's $1.83 billion.

According to the 1997 budget draft the large official trade deficit will only partially be offset by inflows from unclassified cross-border trade, seen at $7.06 billion this year an dropping to $6.50 billion in 1997.

"The fall of inflows form cross-border trade is a result of the process of adjustment of Polish prices to world prices and the lower attractiveness of shopping in Poland for foreigners," the draft said. @

The government expects foreign investment in 1997 to reach $3 billion, of which $1.5 billion is expected to be portfolio investment, including $300 million Eurobonds which the government plans to issue in 1997.

Foreign direct investment in Poland in 1996 is estimated to reach $2.2 billion, twice as much as in 1995. The draft expects portfolio investment at $500 million this year, but gives no comparable figures for 1995.
The budget draft, which assumes a deficit of 2.6 percent of gross domestic product, unchanged tax levels in 1997 and a 5.5 percent GDP growth, was submitted to parliament last week. @

But the final shape of the budget depends on the parliament's decision on 1997 taxes and the government signalled it would amend the draft and propose a 2.8 percent deficit if its planned moderate tax cuts won parliamentary approval.
